docs.title: Climate Toolkit
docs.text:
Location-based climate analysis for agriculture: fetch daily climate data, compute seasonal climatologies and drought indices, assess crop and livestock hazards, and compare periods, data sources, and weather stations — for any point location.

Try it in your browser — no install

The companion Colab notebook installs the package and runs the credential-free examples end-to-end on a free Google-hosted runtime.

docs.title: Install
docs.text: pip install climate-toolkit

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
import climate_toolkit as ct
from datetime import date

df = ct.fetch_climate_data(
    source="nasa_power",              # needs no credentials
    location_coord=(-1.286, 36.817),  # Nairobi
    date_from=date(2020, 1, 1),
    date_to=date(2020, 12, 31),
)
df.head()

nasa_power works with zero setup. For CHIRPS v3 rainfall and CHIRTS-ERA5 daily temperatures, use direct cloud access on Python 3.12+ with climate-toolkit[cloud]. For ERA5-Land, ERA5 and NEX-GDDP, follow Earth Engine setup.

docs.title: What's in the box
docs.text:
Function Purpose fetch_climate_data Daily climate data for a site as a pandas DataFrame analyze_climate_statistics Seasonal climatology, water balance, SPI/SPEI evaluate_hazards Crop & livestock hazard assessment for a season compare_climate_periods Focal year vs. baseline climatology compare_climate_sources Side-by-side gridded dataset comparison download_station_data Daily observations from nearby weather stations compare_station_to_grids Validate gridded data against stations

These seven analyses also have CLI commands. The Python API overview includes run_pipeline for running a whole workflow and backend_policy for controlling data access.

docs.title: About the Climate Toolkit
docs.text:
From a point on the map to climate evidence you can stand behind.

The Climate Toolkit is an open-source tool for anyone working in agroecology and food systems who needs to know what the climate did — or will do — at the places they work. Give it a location and it fetches trusted climate data, works out the growing season, and measures the hazards that matter to crops, livestock, and people.

It was built for a simple reason: the people who most need climate evidence shouldn't have to become climate-data engineers to get it.

Funded by the McKnight Foundation (CRFS programme) and the CGIAR Climate Action Program through AoW1 — the Climate Data Hub, in partnership with AIMS Research and Innovation Centre (AIMS RIC):

docs.title: The problem
docs.text:
Nearly every agroecology project claims to build climate resilience. Very few can show it.

It's not for lack of data — the data exists, in abundance. But it is scattered across dozens of archives, each with its own formats, credentials, and quirks. Joining it to the farm and household records a project already holds takes time, bandwidth, and coding skill that most research and M&E teams don't have to spare. So the climate context stays anecdotal — "it was a dry year" — instead of measured.

The result is a gap between the resilience we claim and the resilience we can prove. That gap weakens reports, proposals, and ultimately the case for agroecology itself.

docs.title: What the toolkit does
docs.text:
No new datasets, no new portal to maintain — one consistent doorway to the open climate data that already exists, with the analysis steps built in.

  • Fetch

    Daily climate data for any point location from CHIRPS, ERA5-Land, NASA POWER, TerraClimate, IMERG, CMIP6 projections, and nearby weather stations — returned as one tidy, analysis-ready table.

  • Understand the season

    Seasonal climatologies, water balance, and drought indices (SPI/SPEI) over the years that matter to a place.

  • Measure the hazards

    Crop- and livestock-relevant risks — heat, drought, waterlogging — assessed across a growing season, with sensible thresholds you can customise.

  • Compare and check

    A hard year against the long-term normal, one dataset against another, or a gridded product against a real weather station.

Because it works from a single point and reuses trusted open data, it stays light, low-cost, and usable where bandwidth is limited. You can run the whole thing in your browser — no installation — via the companion Colab notebook.

docs.title: Who it's for
docs.text:
• Project & M&E teams

    You hold data on farms, practices, and outcomes — but not the climate context to show whether an intervention helped people cope with a hard season. The toolkit adds that context and turns it into a defensible, quantified story for reports and proposals. No coding from scratch.

  • Researchers

    One reproducible interface to the datasets and hazard indicators you use, so you spend less time wrangling sources and more time on the science.

  • Data & support staff

    The multipliers. Learn it once, embed it in your team's everyday workflow, and equip everyone around you.

  • Educators & students

    A real, well-documented, open tool for teaching and learning climate data analysis.

If you work with a place and want to know what its climate has done, is doing, or may do — this is for you.

docs.title: Where we're going
docs.text: We want climate evidence to be a normal, everyday part of agroecological research and practice — not a specialist luxury. Over the longer term that means lowering the technical bar until any motivated team can add solid climate context to their work; consolidating scattered climate-analysis know-how into one open, trustworthy place people build on rather than reinvent; and strengthening the evidence base for agroecology as a climate solution — moving the field from assumed resilience to measured resilience. The toolkit will grow with its users: more crops, more hazards, more regions, more languages, always open, always a public good.

docs.title: Get involved
docs.text:
The toolkit is in active early development (alpha), and it is being shaped by the people who use it. This is the best moment to influence where it goes.

  • Try it

    Open the Colab notebook and run it on a location you care about. No install, no setup.

  • Tell us what's missing

    A bug, a missing crop, a hazard we don't cover, something confusing? Open an issue — every one directly shapes the roadmap.

  • Join the conversation

    Questions, ideas, and show-and-tell live in GitHub Discussions — the home of our growing community of practice.

  • :material-teach:{ .lg .middle } Learn with us

    A short, practical training course is in development — built around real datasets, including your own, for people who work with project data but aren't necessarily coders. Course materials will live here.

docs.title: Datasets
docs.text:
All datasets accepted by the source argument of fetch_climate_data and the other API functions.

Auth: "EE" sources are served through Google Earth Engine and need a one-time setup. "None" sources work with no credentials.

source Dataset Type Native resolution Coverage Variables Auth era5_land ERA5-Land daily aggregates Reanalysis 0.1° (~11 km) 1950-01-02–near present precip, tmax/tmin/tmean, humidity, wind, solar EE era_5 ERA5 daily Reanalysis 0.25° (~28 km) 1979-01-02 – 2020-07-09 (static asset; live coverage checked at runtime) precip, tmax/tmin, wind EE terraclimate TerraClimate Monthly climate & water balance 1/24° (~4 km) 1958–present, monthly precip, tmax/tmin, wind, solar, soil moisture EE imerg GPM IMERG v07 Satellite precipitation 0.1° (~11 km) 2000–present precip EE chirps_v2 (alias chirps) CHIRPS v2 daily Blended satellite–gauge precipitation 0.05° (~5.5 km) 1981–present precip EE chirps_v3_daily_rnl CHIRPS v3 daily final/RNL Blended satellite–gauge precipitation 0.05° (~5.5 km) 1981–provider latest precip None with cloud extra; optional EE fallback chirts_era5 CHIRTS-ERA5 daily CHIRTS-calibrated ERA5 temperature 0.05° (~5.5 km) Hosted 1981–provider latest tmax/tmin None with cloud extra chirts (deprecated) CHIRTS daily Satellite–station temperature 0.05° (~5.5 km) 1983–2016 tmax/tmin EE cmip_6 NASA GDDP-CMIP6 Downscaled projections 0.25° (~27 km) historical + scenarios precip, tmax/tmin EE nex_gddp NEX-GDDP-CMIP6 Downscaled projections (per GCM × SSP) 0.25° (~27 km) historical to 2014-12-31; scenarios from 2015-01-01 precip, tmax/tmin, humidity EE nasa_power NASA POWER daily Reanalysis-derived point API ~0.5° 1984–present precip, tmax/tmin/tmean, humidity None tamsat TAMSAT v3.1 African rainfall (satellite) 0.05° (~4 km), Africa only 1983–present precip, soil moisture None ghcn_daily GHCN-Daily Weather station observations point station-dependent precip, tmax/tmin None gsod NOAA GSOD Weather station observations point station-dependent precip, tmax/tmin None soil_grid ISRIC SoilGrids / OpenLandMap Static soil properties 250 m static texture, bulk density, pH, organic carbon, CEC EE hwsd FAO HWSD v2 Static soil properties ~1 km static root depth, AWC, drainage, bulk density EE

era5_land is backed by ERA5-Land

Former keys agera_5 and agera5 are deprecated aliases through 0.2.x. Calls using them warn and return the same ERA5-Land data; use era5_land for new requests. Existing cache directories remain compatible. The era5_land source reads the Earth Engine asset ECMWF/ERA5_LAND/DAILY_AGGR (ERA5-Land daily aggregates), which shares ERA5-Land's 0.1° grid. It is the recommended default for recent daily data because of its variable breadth and continuously updated coverage. This is distinct from Copernicus AgERA5. The listed start date follows the upstream GEE catalogue; individual request coverage must still be verified. Official CDS ARCO access requires a CDS key and is shelved, with no integrated alternative backend yet.

Cloud dependencies, provider controls and CHIRTS migration: direct cloud access.

docs.title: Choosing a source
docs.text:
• Recent daily data, most variables → era5_land (needs EE).
  • Zero-setup start → nasa_power (no credentials, coarser grid).
  • Best precipitation detail → chirps_v3_daily_rnl (0.05°, precip only); pair with a temperature source via precip_source / temp_source.
  • Future climate → nex_gddp with model (e.g. 'GFDL-ESM4') and scenario (e.g. 'ssp245'); pass models="all" on the CLI for ensembles.
  • Ground truth / validation → ghcn_daily or gsod stations, then compare_station_to_grids.
  • Soil inputs for water balance → fetched automatically by the hazard and statistics functions; request explicitly via SoilVariable members.

docs.title: Variables
docs.text:
Request variables with ClimateVariable enum members:

from climate_toolkit.fetch_data.source_data.sources.utils.models import (
    ClimateVariable,
    SoilVariable,
)

ClimateVariable: precipitation, max_temperature, min_temperature, mean_temperature, rainfall, wind_speed, solar_radiation, humidity, soil_moisture.

SoilVariable (for soil_grid / hwsd): root_depth, available_water_capacity, drainage, bulk_density, coarse_fragments, field_capacity, wilting_point, ph, sand_content, clay_content, silt_content, organic_carbon, organic_carbon_stock, cation_exchange_capacity, soil_moisture.

Not every source provides every variable (see the table above). Requests outside legacy source coverage windows may be clipped with a warning. Direct cloud requests require the full window and fail over or raise an error when it is incomplete.

docs.title: Direct cloud access and provider fallback
docs.text: Architecture reference: package architecture. Implementation tracks issues #176, #177 and #178.

docs.title: Install and fetch
docs.text:
Direct backends require Python 3.12+ and the optional cloud dependencies:

pip install 'climate-toolkit[cloud]'
# From a checkout:
uv sync --extra cloud

The base toolkit still supports Python 3.10+. On older Python versions, direct cloud fetches report the requirement; existing explicit GEE paths remain available.

from datetime import date
import climate_toolkit as ct

rain = ct.fetch_climate_data(
    "chirps_v3_daily_rnl",
    location_coord=(-1.286, 36.817),
    date_from=date(2020, 1, 1), date_to=date(2020, 12, 31),
    allow_gee=False,
)
temperature = ct.fetch_climate_data(
    "chirts_era5",
    location_coord=(-1.286, 36.817),
    date_from=date(2020, 1, 1), date_to=date(2020, 12, 31),
    allow_gee=False,
)
print(rain.attrs["data_provenance"])

sites=[("Nairobi", -1.286, 36.817), ...] or sites_csv=... uses the same provider policy and groups lazy point reads into shared storage chunks. workers bounds concurrency (1–8 for direct access).

docs.title: Products and providers
docs.text:
Source Automatic provider order Coverage discovery chirps_v3_daily_rnl Complete compatible cache first; Dynamical final, Hugging Face, permitted GEE Actual time coordinates; full requested range required chirts_era5 Complete cache first; Hugging Face Actual time coordinates; hosted archive starts 1981

Dynamical used less bandwidth in every measured one-year CHIRPS layout. A 2020 Nairobi request used 3.39 MB across 20 requests on Dynamical and 21.54 MB across 26 on Hugging Face. Both cached repeats made zero upstream requests. Dynamical's final archive also had more recent coverage at validation. Hugging Face can be faster for short requests. See the CHIRPS transport benchmark for larger workloads and limits. Select backend="huggingface" or backend="dynamical" explicitly when needed. An explicit backend does not silently switch providers.

The CHIRPS adapters both read v3 final/RNL. Dynamical preliminary is SAT and is excluded. Neither CHIRPS v2 nor another rainfall product is a mirror fallback.

Dynamical stores a daily-average precipitation rate; the adapter converts it to mm/day. Hugging Face CF scaling is decoded once by xarray. The mirrors apply different rounding: comparisons must allow documented packing error, and daily threshold counts can differ. One returned request uses a single provider revision; there is no per-day stitching across providers.

For CHIRPS v3, a check against Earth Engine's native grid compared 543 daily values per mirror at Nairobi, Ouagadougou and Cusco in December–February 2019/20 and 2025/26. Maximum daily differences were 0.041 mm for Dynamical and 0.050 mm for Hugging Face (rounded up). At a strict wet-day cutoff of >1 mm, classifications differed on zero and three site-days, respectively. For threshold-sensitive comparisons, select one backend and keep its revision with the results. See the reference comparison and reproduction instructions.

CHIRTS-ERA5 is the successor for new temperature workflows. The old chirts key (CHIRTS-daily, 1983–2016) is deprecated and warns when selected. Its existing adapter is retained only for explicit legacy reproduction; automatic fallback now uses CHIRTS-ERA5. Existing keys/caches are never relabeled or combined. The chirps_v2+chirts shorthand retains its historical meaning.

CHIRTS-ERA5 improves temporal coverage, not guaranteed accuracy at every site. Its producer publishes ongoing monitoring data at approximately five-day latency; the mirror can lag. Both old CHIRTS-daily and CHIRTS-ERA5 use ERA5 information, with different constructions. Do not interpret this as a simple file-host change.

The Hugging Face mirror stores Tmax and Tmin in steps of 0.1 °C. Heat-day counts use the decoded temperature, including days exactly at 35 °C (NTx35) or 40 °C (NTx40). For example, an original Tmax of 34.96 °C rounds to 35.0 °C and counts toward NTx35 in the mirror. Seasonal means also use the decoded values.

Check local station bias before using absolute temperature thresholds. Across 1994–95 and 2023–24, CHIRTS-ERA5 daily minima averaged 3.2–4.3 °C warmer than the Nairobi station and 3.3–3.8 °C warmer than the Cusco station on matched dates. At Ouagadougou in 2023–24, the grid missed 30 of the station's 349 days at or above 35 °C and added six. Station coverage varies by site and variable.

Budget for bandwidth on long requests. Thirty years of daily Tmax and Tmin at Nairobi took 137 seconds and 1.47 GB on a cold read. The cached repeat took 0.07 seconds with zero network requests. The same window across 10 or 100 dispersed sites exceeded the default 4 GiB decoded-work limit. Group nearby sites or request shorter windows for dispersed studies. See the station comparisons and transport measurements.

docs.title: Paired workflows and GEE controls
docs.text:
with ct.backend_policy(allow_gee=False):
    result = ct.analyze_climate_statistics(
        location_coord=(-1.286, 36.817), start_year=2020, end_year=2020,
        source="paired", precip_source="chirps_v3_daily_rnl",
        temp_source="chirts_era5", fixed_season="03-01:05-31",
    )

climate-toolkit fetch --source chirps_v3_daily_rnl --no-gee \
  --lat -1.286 --lon 36.817 --start 2020-01-01 --end 2020-12-31

climate-toolkit stats --no-gee --source paired \
  --precip-source chirps_v3_daily_rnl --temp-source chirts_era5 \
  --location=-1.286,36.817 --start-year 2020 --end-year 2020 \
  --fixed-season 03-01:05-31

The unified CLI accepts --backend and --no-gee on all commands; standalone fetch accepts them too. Other standalone commands can use CLIMATE_TOOLKIT_ALLOW_GEE=false and CLIMATE_TOOLKIT_BACKEND=auto environment settings. Python contexts nest and library model-worker processes inherit policy. User-created threads/processes should enter their own context.

Normal historical auto retains CHIRPS v3 + the existing era5_land source (ERA5-Land, not the distinct AgERA5 product) for companion variables. Its final temperature fallback is now CHIRTS-ERA5. With GEE prohibited, historical auto directly selects CHIRPS v3 + CHIRTS-ERA5. This pair supplies precipitation and Tmax/Tmin only: it does not supply humidity, wind, radiation or soil data. Existing workflow requirements for those inputs still apply. Human-heat metadata marks absent companion inputs as null rather than attributing them to CHIRTS-ERA5.

Explicit backend selection applies to cloud-enabled sources; other datasets keep existing routes, subject to the global GEE prohibition. Choosing dynamical for a CHIRTS-ERA5 request fails because no such adapter exists. Use auto for mixed-source paired workflows. Automatic GEE fallback never opens an interactive authentication flow; pre-existing setup is required.

docs.title: Full pipeline
docs.text:
run_pipeline carries one explicit pair and provider policy through daily fetch, climatology, source comparison, seasonal statistics, crop hazards and period comparison. This short verification example uses a two-year climatology; use an appropriate longer baseline for scientific normals, subject to the performance limits below.

result = ct.run_pipeline(
    name="Nairobi", location_coord=(-1.286, 36.817),
    source="paired", precip_source="chirps_v3_daily_rnl", temp_source="chirts_era5",
    allow_gee=False, workers=2,
    start_year=2020, end_year=2020,
    climatology_baseline=(2019, 2020),
    fixed_season="03-01:05-31", crop_name="maize",
    run_compare_sources=True,
    compare_sources_list=["paired", "chirps_v3_daily_rnl", "chirts_era5"],
    run_compare_periods=True,
    baseline_start=2019, baseline_end=2019, focal_year=2020,
    output_dir="outputs/nairobi_pipeline",
)
print(result.summary)
assert not result.errors, result.errors

source="auto", allow_gee=False selects this pair too. backend="auto" is appropriate for mixed rainfall/temperature sources; Dynamical has no temperature adapter. ee_project_id, when supplied for permitted GEE paths, is forwarded rather than discarded.

Each site's directory contains daily.csv with its metadata sidecar, JSON stage reports and status.json; run root contains summary.csv and metadata.json. Daily source-comparison exports live in that site's source_comparison/ folder. Check status and completed_steps before consuming a report. Returned errors and partial source comparisons fail the stage; unsuccessful reruns remove obsolete pipeline JSON reports. Individual source-comparison exports may remain as diagnostic partial output and are not proof that the stage completed.

Direct climatology requires all requested years and rejects QC failures; it does not silently compute a shortened baseline. Paired climatology is also available through the CLI:

climate-toolkit climatology --no-gee --source paired \
  --precip-source chirps_v3_daily_rnl --temp-source chirts_era5 \
  --location=-1.286,36.817 --start-year 2019 --end-year 2020 \
  --format json --output outputs/climatology.json --output-dir ""

docs.title: Data integrity, caches and limits
docs.text:
• Raw frames expose decoded source-native columns, QC summaries and provenance. Transformed/preprocessed frames use canonical names. Direct data retains its precision; existing generic filling and heuristic unit conversions are bypassed.
  • Missing/infinite values, negative precipitation, temperatures outside -90 to 60 °C, or Tmin greater than Tmax prevent direct data from entering analysis. Inspect stage="raw" to diagnose. These gross screening limits do not establish scientific accuracy. Invalid scientific values are not treated as outages.
  • Transport/provider failures, stale coverage, missing dates/variables or incompatible metadata can trigger another eligible mirror. Partial date ranges are never silently accepted. Ocean/out-of-domain points do not become nearby land points.
  • Annual request chunks live under outputs/cache/direct_cloud/v2/<source>/<backend>/ (or the supplied root). Checksummed JSON preserves float precision, column order, requested coordinates, selected cells, units, provider revision and dates. Writes are atomic. Complete cache hits need no metadata/authentication calls, even when the cached provider was a fallback. An interrupted read can reuse matching-revision chunks; a new revision causes replacement rather than mixing revisions. refresh_cache=True opts into current upstream data. Existing GEE caches are separate and untouched. Consecutive missing years load in batches of at most five years, sharing source chunks across calendar boundaries. Each completed batch saves separate annual records, so a later outage can resume from those records at the same revision.
  • Fetch and dataset-comparison CSV/JSON exports write a .metadata.json sidecar. Statistics, period comparisons, hazard assessments and station diagnostics carry additive data_provenance fields. Cache inventory includes direct_cloud.
  • Metadata HTTP calls use bounded timeouts and retries; data transports have bounded request timeouts. Default estimated source-chunk work budget is 4 GiB per provider request. This is decoded source size, not measured network bytes. Exceeding it skips that provider. Set CLIMATE_TOOLKIT_MAX_DECODED_BYTES explicitly to change the budget. Long or widely dispersed jobs can still take minutes.

Reproduce live measurements with scripts/benchmark_direct_cloud.py. Its default 90-second per-case deadline is a benchmark gate, not the library's whole-job timeout. Ordinary tests use offline fixtures; live benchmarking is opt-in.

CHIRTS-ERA5 currently has one integrated direct provider. CHC GeoTIFF/NetCDF archives are independent originals, but daily files and observed partial-read failures need further work before they qualify as efficient automatic backups. The 2026-11-02 probe found a rejected current-year Tmax NetCDF and a Tmin file ending in September; the EWX catalogue exposed only pentadal/monthly aggregates. Historical NetCDF point reads also exceeded the short-query performance target. The November 10 check also found same-cell daily Tmin differences of 0.20–2.18 °C between the October 21 CHC original and the pinned Hugging Face mirror. These exceed the mirror's 0.05 °C packing tolerance. Revision equivalence must be established before the original can serve as an automatic fallback. Reproduce bounded range probes with scripts/probe_chc_backup.py (requires the investigation-only h5py dependency). See the backup investigation. Tracked in #179; credential-free ERA5-Land companion variables are tracked in #180. The ERA5-Land access audit found authenticated CDS ARCO stores as a candidate, but live metadata access rejected the configured key. CDS work is shelved because credentials are required; no ERA5-Land cloud backend is enabled. CDS hourly flow fields also need explicit day-boundary aggregation to match existing GEE results.
